title: Mobility data that points to a home
scenario: Data scientist Aigerim Seitkali at a Nur-Sultan transport agency prepares to release an open dataset of anonymised bus-card trips. A university colleague shows that the combination of a rare night-shift route and two daily stops identifies a small number of riders, including a woman who visits a women's shelter. Delaying release would stall a planned fare reform study with real public value. Aigerim must decide how to publish.
options: Release the dataset with the rare routes generalised and sensitive stops removed, accepting a loss in analytic detail.
Release it as planned, since individual risk is small and the transport planning benefit is large.
Restrict access to vetted researchers under a data-use agreement, which protects riders but reduces openness.

title: Linking a hospital file to the electoral roll
scenario: Health economist Dr. Beatriz Carvalho in Lisbon is given de-identified hospital discharge records. She realises that joining them with the public voter list on birth date, postcode and sex would re-identify many patients, letting her study which diagnoses affect voting. The linkage would be valuable, but the data-use agreement forbids attempts to identify individuals. A reviewer might never know. She must decide whether to test it.
options: Run the linkage on a tiny sample only to demonstrate the risk, then tell the data provider.
Do nothing and report the vulnerability to the data provider without testing it.
Run the full linkage under a revised agreement that she negotiates, accepting delays and possible refusal.

title: A school district asks for children's names
scenario: Analytics lead Marcus Whitfield at a US ed-tech firm is asked by a district to supply a list of students whom his dropout model flags as highest risk, so counsellors can reach out. The firm's contract says data is used only in aggregate. Parents were not told of individual predictions, and labels might stigmatise children. The model is imperfect, with many false alarms. Marcus must decide whether to share the list.
options: Share the list with careful safeguards, since helping at-risk students is the system's whole purpose.
Refuse and offer only aggregate patterns, honouring the contract and avoiding labels.
Share it after notifying parents and offering opt-out, which delays help and may reach fewer students.

title: Genealogy database and a cold case
scenario: Forensic geneticist Dr. Ingeborg Haugen at a Norwegian police lab is asked to upload a crime-scene DNA profile to a public hobbyist genealogy database to identify a decades-old killer. Users agreed to share data for family-finding, not policing, though the site's terms permit law-enforcement use only with consent. Relatives of the victim plead for a breakthrough. A match would implicate relatives of users who never agreed. She must decide.
options: Upload the profile, as the crime is serious and the database terms are arguably flexible.
Decline until each database user can opt in and the legal framework is clear, accepting the case may stay cold.
Seek a court order and notify the database's operator transparently, which is slower but accountable.
tension: justice for victims vs. genetic privacy of relatives

title: Employee Wi-Fi logs for a wellbeing study
scenario: Organisational psychologist Dr. Chidinma Okeke in Port Harcourt partners with an oil services firm to study work stress using badge swipes and Wi-Fi connection logs. The data would reveal where staff spend breaks, including prayer rooms and the clinic. Employees were told only that 'analytics' may be used. Management promises anonymity but holds the key to link IDs. Chidinma must decide how to design the study.
options: Proceed with the logs after removing location data for sensitive rooms, trusting management's anonymity promise.
Decline the log data and use an opt-in survey instead, accepting weaker measurement.
Insist that an independent third party holds the linkage key before she receives any data, delaying the project.

title: Breach notice for a mental health registry
scenario: Registry manager Dr. Ewa Kowalczyk in Gdańsk discovers that a postdoc's laptop, containing a pseudonymised file of 12,000 patients in a psychosis registry, was stolen on a train. The file is encrypted but the password was a simple one. Notifying all patients could cause panic and drive people out of care. The regulator's notification clock is running. Ewa must decide how to respond.
options: Notify the regulator and all affected patients immediately and honestly, accepting the possible loss of trust.
Notify the regulator but wait to inform patients until the risk of actual access is assessed.
Notify the regulator and patients through their treating clinicians with personal support, slower but gentler.

title: Selling anonymised diagnoses to insurers
scenario: Chief data officer Samira Qureshi at a private diagnostic lab chain in Karachi is offered a large contract to supply an insurer with 'anonymised' test result patterns by neighbourhood. She knows that in small areas, patterns could effectively identify families with rare conditions, and insurers could raise premiums or deny cover. The revenue would fund subsidised tests for poor patients. She must decide whether to sign.
options: Sign with contractual bans on re-identification and underwriting use, trusting the safeguards.
Decline, since the risk of discrimination to vulnerable families outweighs the revenue.
Offer the insurer only broad city-level aggregates at a lower price, reducing both risk and income.
tension: subsidising care vs. risk of discrimination

title: Social media scraping for a protest study
scenario: Political scientist Dr. Lucía Fernández in Buenos Aires wants to study how protest movements organise, scraping public posts from thousands of accounts. Some users are in neighbouring countries where protesting is criminalised. Posts are public but writers likely never expected scholarly analysis, and quoted text can be traced by search. Her university's board treats public data as exempt. She must decide how to handle the data.
options: Collect and analyse the public posts, report only aggregate patterns and paraphrase any quotes.
Limit the study to accounts of public figures and organisations, excluding private citizens.
Contact a sample of users for permission, accepting a much smaller and different dataset.
tension: research value vs. risk to activists

title: The wearable data a coach wants
scenario: Sports scientist Dr. Henrik Vogt at a German football academy collects heart-rate and sleep data from teenage players for a research project on overtraining. The head coach asks to see individual data to pick teams, and parents have not been told. Players hope to get contracts and fear saying no. The study has parental consent for research only. Henrik must decide what to share.
options: Share only team-level summaries with the coach, protecting individual players from selection pressure.
Share individual data with the coach, since it may prevent injuries and the club is responsible for the players.
Give each player their own data and let them choose whether to share it, with parental involvement.

title: A dataset of voices from a language at risk
scenario: Linguist Dr. Tāwhiri Parata in Rotorua records elders speaking a nearly lost dialect, with consent for archival and scholarly use. A tech company now wants the recordings to train a speech model, offering money for community language classes. Some elders approve; others say their voices should not feed a product. Several speakers are deceased, and their families disagree. Tāwhiri must decide on the licence.
options: Grant the licence with revenue-sharing, since the funded classes may keep the language alive.
Refuse any commercial licence, keeping the recordings for the community and scholars only.
License only recordings from consenting living speakers and families, leaving a thin dataset.

title: Smart-meter data and a landlord
scenario: Energy researcher Dr. Sibongile Dlamini in Durban holds smart-meter readings from 8,000 households, shared under a pledge not to disclose individual data. A municipal fraud officer requests records for a few addresses suspected of illegal connections, which cost the city money and endanger neighbours. Disclosure would breach her pledge but is within the officer's legal powers. Sibongile must decide how to respond.
options: Comply with the lawful request, since illegal connections cause real harm and the law compels her.
Refuse and defend the confidentiality pledge in court if needed, protecting participant trust.
Offer to share only anonymised consumption patterns that may help detect fraud without naming households.

title: Genomic data from a small island
scenario: Bioinformatician Dr. Mele Fifita in Tonga leads a diabetes genomics project drawing on most of an island's 1,200 residents. The funder requires deposit into an international open-access database. In so small a population, even stripped data is almost identifying, and the genetic risk could affect insurance or marriage prospects. Refusing may cost the grant. She must decide how to deposit.
options: Deposit openly as the funder demands, with participants told of the residual risk.
Deposit to a controlled-access database only, risking a dispute with the funder.
Withdraw the grant rather than release the data, protecting the island but ending the project.

title: Reusing a smartphone survey from a refugee camp
scenario: NGO analyst Yohannes Tesfaye in Addis Ababa holds phone survey data from refugees about health and journeys, collected to plan services. A university team wants it to study migration routes, which could be used by smuggling investigators or border agencies. Respondents were told it was for service planning only. Sharing could bring funding and visibility. Yohannes must decide how to respond.
options: Share the data after removing locations and dates that reveal routes, accepting some analytic loss.
Decline, since respondents consented only to service planning.
Offer to run the university's analysis in-house and share only results, keeping raw data under his control.
tension: research benefit vs. risk to migrants

title: Facial images in a dementia detection project
scenario: Machine learning engineer Priyanka Deshpande in Pune is building a tool to spot early cognitive decline from short video clips taken in memory clinics. The clips contain faces and home environments. Consent covered diagnosis, not model training. A hospital administrator urges quick use of the archive, saying the benefit to patients outweighs paperwork. Priyanka must decide whether to start training.
options: Train on the archive with face blurring and ethics approval for retrospective use, accepting some loss of signal.
Contact patients and carers for new consent before training, slowing the project and shrinking the data.
Train now on the full video, noting that the hospital owns the archive and the benefit is substantial.

title: A teenager's search history in a research export
scenario: Data engineer Olivier Mbeki at a Kinshasa telecom research lab discovers that a shared dataset for studying internet use contains unusually distinct search queries tied to device IDs. One teen's records suggest he is looking up information about sexuality, which in his community could bring serious harm. The dataset is already with five partner labs. Olivier must decide what to do.
options: Alert partners to quarantine the dataset and recall it, accepting a messy and embarrassing process.
Quietly strip the sensitive queries from the master copy and re-issue it without comment.
Raise the issue with the ethics board and await its advice before any change, accepting continued exposure meanwhile.

title: The postcode that identified a donor
scenario: Epidemiology lecturer Dr. Annelies De Smet in Ghent teaches a class using a de-identified cancer registry extract. A student realises that she can identify her own neighbour, a public figure, from rare tumour type, age and postcode. The student wants to flag it; the registry head says the extract meets legal standards and complaints would hurt the programme. Annelies must decide how to respond.
options: Report the re-identification to the registry's data protection officer and suspend use of the extract.
Tell the student to keep it confidential and continue teaching, since the extract complies with the standard.
Replace the extract with a coarser version for teaching, quietly fixing the risk without formal report.

title: Facial recognition on village census photos
scenario: Demographer Dr. Ramón Quispe-Mamani in La Paz holds ID-style photos taken for a census in highland communities. A computer vision startup offers to help detect duplicate registrations that waste welfare payments, using face matching. The technology could also be used for policing or tracking, and the communities have not been consulted. Welfare budgets are tight. Ramón must decide whether to grant access.
options: Grant access for duplicate detection only, under a strict contract and audit rights.
Decline until the communities have been consulted and agree, even if fraud continues.
Run the matching himself with the startup's open software, keeping photos in-house but limiting scrutiny.

title: Cell tower data in an epidemic
scenario: Public health analyst Dr. Nadia Rahman in Dhaka is offered aggregate call-detail records by a mobile operator to track movements during a cholera outbreak. The operator's legal team notes that the data can be de-aggregated in small villages, and the government has previously used phone data against opposition activists. Faster tracking might save lives within weeks. Nadia must decide whether to accept.
options: Accept with village-level aggregation thresholds and a sunset date for deletion.
Decline, as the risk of political misuse in this context cannot be reliably controlled.
Accept but require an independent oversight panel with civil society members, slowing access.

title: Open-sourcing a leaked patient file
scenario: Journalist-researcher Katarzyna Zielinska, working in Warsaw as a data analyst for a transparency group, receives a leaked spreadsheet from a private clinic showing patient names alongside fertility treatments and payment amounts. It shows the clinic overbilling the national insurer. Publishing the full file would prove the fraud but expose thousands of private medical details. She must decide what to publish.
options: Publish the redacted billing patterns only, sacrificing some proof strength to protect patients.
Publish the full file, because the fraud is large and verification requires the raw records.
Give the file to the regulator and prosecutors, publishing nothing, and trusting the authorities to act.

title: A volunteer's genealogical reveal
scenario: Citizen-science coordinator Brigitte Landry in Montreal runs a project in which volunteers upload DNA kits to trace migrations. A volunteer's matches reveal that two of her cousins are half-siblings via an affair that the older generation hid, and the cousins are about to be notified automatically through the platform's relative-finder. Brigitte can disable the notification for this cluster. The families do not know. She must decide.
options: Let the standard notification proceed, since participants agreed to relative matching.
Disable it for these individuals and let the volunteer decide how to share the discovery.
Message both cousins in advance with a warning and counselling resources before notification goes out.
tension: right to know vs. harm of sudden disclosure

title: Ride-hailing logs and a divorce subpoena
scenario: Research lead Teodoro Villanueva at a Manila mobility startup runs a study of commuter safety using anonymised trip logs. A family court subpoena asks for any data on a specific user's pickups to be handed over in a custody dispute. Teodoro's pipeline has pseudonyms but an engineer can re-link them. The user claims the logs would be misused by an abusive ex. Teodoro must decide how to respond.
options: Comply with the subpoena after notifying the user and letting her challenge it.
Refuse, citing the research confidentiality terms, and fight in court at the company's expense.
Hand over only the narrow timeframe requested, with sensitive locations removed, and tell the court of the limits.

title: Re-identifying a published prison cohort
scenario: Criminologist Dr. Gustavo Almeida in Salvador has access to a published, anonymised dataset on former prisoners' employment outcomes. A reporter asks him whether individuals could be found, and he realises a curious student could do it using news archives. If he publishes a demonstration, authors may fix the problem; the former prisoners could also face stigma if the method spreads. He must decide how to disclose.
options: Inform the dataset's authors privately and give them time to fix it before any public mention.
Publish a general warning paper about the vulnerability without naming the dataset.
Decline the reporter's question altogether, leaving the weakness unreported.

title: Children's drawings from a war zone
scenario: Psychologist Dr. Oksana Melnyk in Lviv collected children's drawings about displacement for a trauma study, with signed parental permission for research. A museum abroad wants to exhibit them with names and ages, promising to raise funds for the children's shelters. Some parents are enthusiastic; others have moved and cannot be reached. Some drawings reveal home addresses. Oksana must decide what to allow.
options: Allow the exhibition for children whose parents consent, with names removed and address details cropped.
Decline entirely, since the original permission covered research only.
Allow an exhibit of anonymous composites rather than original drawings, preserving the message but altering the material.
tension: advocacy and funding vs. original consent

title: Smart speaker transcripts in a care home
scenario: Gerontology researcher Dr. Ingrid Vandenberg in Pretoria tests voice assistants in a care home, recording daily requests to learn how residents use them. A resident's recordings reveal repeated phone calls to a lawyer about changing her will, and signs that her son may be pressuring her. Residents consented to speech research only. Ingrid has no mandate as a social worker. She must decide whether to act.
options: Tell the care home's manager about the recordings and her concern, breaching the research promise to protect the resident.
Keep the recordings confidential and encourage the resident to talk to staff herself.
Consult the ethics committee quickly about limits to confidentiality before doing anything else.
tension: researcher role vs. duty of care

title: Anonymised taxi tracks and a celebrity
scenario: Urban analyst Wei Zhang in Chengdu publishes a visualisation of anonymised taxi routes to show evening patterns. A local blogger spots a repeated drop-off near a clinic and, by cross-referencing a news story, claims to identify a local official's regular treatment visits. Wei's city department says the data complied with rules. Wei can pull the dataset or leave it up. He must decide.
options: Withdraw the visualisation and dataset immediately and review the anonymisation, accepting the loss of public value.
Leave it up, since the blogger's claim is speculation and the data meets the legal standard.
Replace it with a version that blurs timestamps and destinations, and notify the people who downloaded the original.
tension: transparency of research vs. incidental harm
